newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU opts for caution on Albania crisis.
newsitem.headline: EU opts for caution on Albania crisis.

text.p: The European Union on Saturday offered a muted response to Albania's plunge into anarchy, opting for caution rather than action.

The bloc's 15 members, still stung by criticism for indecision over the Yugoslav conflict the last time violence flared on their eastern doorstep, were split on what to do to help calm tensions in Europe's poorest country.
The divisions emerged as EU foreign ministers met for informal talks in Apeldoorn in the eastern Netherlands.
One camp, driven by France and Italy, favoured putting together an international force of several thousand troops to try and restore law and order in Albania.

Others questioned the point of sending soldiers into a country where disparate rag-tag gangs have looted military depots and where the price of a Kalashnikov rifle has more than halved in less than a week.

"There is no way any military commander in any serious western country would envisage sending two to three thousand troops into Albania to try and restore law and order under the current circumstances," one British diplomat said.
Germany, too, was sceptical about sending in peacekeepers.
"You have to ask whether you can really intervene whenever anarchy erupts," Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told Germany's SAT1TV channel.
Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, however, earlier said his country, the current OSCE president, favoured a combined multinational force.
OSCE mediator Franz Vranitzky, returned from Friday's talks with Albanian leaders to say that there was no alternative to foreign intervention to halt Albania's descent into chaos.

His call was echoed by Carl Bildt, the international community's Bosnia representative, who said in a statement on Saturady that Europe's failure to act would make current discussion on joint foreign and security policy look "pathetic".
In Paris, French Prime Minister Alain Juppe urged a greater political role for the EU in organising presidential and general elections in Albania.

"Europe must support...a political project for national reconciliation. We should help place what Albanian political forces remain around a negotiating table so that real... elections are organised and the Albanians can express themselves," he said.
There were also conflicting EU signals on the status of Albania's President Sali Berisha, with several calls for him to quit as a first step towards calming tensions in Albania.
"I'm sure that if President Berisha was to step down that would in some ways improve the situation in Albania," Helveg Petersen said.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said in a newspaper interview that he no longer saw Berisha as a key player and said his fate was in the hands of the Balkan state's new premier.
"It's up to Prime Minister (Bashkim) Fino to assess what Berisha's role might now be," he told La Repubblica.
However, British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind opposed any political manoeuvring to oust Berisha.
"It is not for the West or for the international community to take sides as between Mr Berisha and anyone else, that is for the Albanians ultimately to decide," he said.

Ministers attending the Apeldoorn meeting were also discussing plans to admit former communist states and were due on Sunday to turn their attention to prickly relations with Turkey, recently snubbed by EU Christian Democrat leaders.
